finding: The legacy-fallback trigger is described two different ways. §3.4 falls back to the stored clean flag "whose recorded findings are unavailable," while Test 5 (§11 #5) phrases the identical fallback as a round "before this release (no severity breakdown)." These are distinct conditions: a pre-release round can have findings recorded but lacking per-finding severity. §3.4/§4.3 say the clean decision reads each surviving finding's severity, but leaves undefined how a severity-less-yet-present finding is classified (blocking vs non-blocking) — so it is untestable whether such a round recomputes or honors its stored flag.
suggestion: Define the fallback on one observable condition (e.g. "a round whose recorded findings lack a per-finding severity field falls back to its stored clean flag") and state how a finding with a missing/unknown severity is treated if recompute is attempted; align §3.4 wording and Test 5 to that single condition.

finding: The predicate that flips a round from live recompute to stored-clean-flag fallback is stated two incompatible ways. §3.4 says fallback applies to a round 'whose recorded findings are unavailable'; Test 5 (§11 item 5) says the trigger is a round with 'no severity breakdown.' These are different conditions — a legacy round can have its findings recorded yet carry no by_severity/per-finding severity. The implementer cannot tell whether 'legacy' is detected by absence of findings or absence of severity data, and the two choices classify real rounds differently.
suggestion: Pin one detection criterion (e.g. 'a round is legacy iff its recorded findings carry no per-finding severity' OR 'iff no findings file is present') and use identical wording in §3.4 and Test 5.

finding: next_action is required to name EXACTLY ONE command, but branch 2 ("convergence-blocking unresolved findings present") enumerates three alternative commands — `--resolve-all <status>` for the batch case, `--resolve <idx>` for one, and `tp review --verify --findings` for "disputed" ones — with no rule for which one is selected. "Disputed" is never defined as an observable round property, so the selector is unknowable. Test 14 accepts "names resolve/verify" (a slash), which is itself not a deterministic assertion. Two engineers testing the same blocking-findings state could assert --resolve-all vs --verify and both claim conformance.
suggestion: Pin a single deterministic command for branch 2 (e.g. always name `--resolve-all` for >1 blocking finding, `--resolve <idx>` for exactly one, and never emit --verify from next_action), and change Test 14 to assert one exact command string rather than "resolve/verify".

finding: §8.1 promises next_action for "the audit equivalents" of --status/--record, and §8.2 item 1 explicitly names the audit forward command ("audit: proceed"). But §8.2 items 2 and 3 supply only review commands: item 2 names tp review --resolve-all/--resolve/--verify, and item 3 names tp set --workflow checks keyed on a mechanize_candidates class that §8.2 describes as a review --record signal. Audit findings are PASS/FAIL rows that are not resolved via --resolve/--resolve-all, audit has no --verify path, and mechanize_candidates is not stated to exist on audit --record. So for the common non-converged audit round (open FAIL findings) neither branch 2 nor 3 yields a command, yet §8.2 requires next_action to 'name exactly one command'. Test 14 exercises only the review next_action, so the audit next_action is both under-defined and untested.
suggestion: Define the audit-loop next_action branches explicitly: e.g. a non-converged audit round names 'run another audit round to fix and re-record' with the concrete audit command, and state whether mechanize_candidates/register-a-check applies to audit at all. Add an acceptance test for the audit next_action mirroring Test 14.

finding: next_action's entire purpose is to spare an agent from re-deriving the next command via the §8.2 precedence (convergence state, blocking-finding presence, mechanize_candidates). But §8.4 strips next_action under --compact — the same sentence calls this the 'always-on' path — so the field is absent exactly where agents operate by default. The flags §8.4 keeps under compact (harness_stale, nonblocking_open, accepted_open) do not answer 'decompose vs resolve vs register-a-check', so a compact-path agent must recompute the very thing next_action was added to hand it, and the round-trip/token savings the feature promises land only on the rarely-used non-compact path.
suggestion: Either keep next_action under --compact (it is a single short command string that changes the agent's very next call — decision-critical by tp's own §8.4 test, not 're-derivable prose'), or state explicitly that an agent wanting the named action must request --no-compact and justify why the primary AX beneficiary is expected to opt out of the default path.

finding: §3.3 says an unrecognized review_converge_on value 'from tp set --workflow, the environment, or .tp/config.json is rejected as a usage error (exit 2)', implying an invalid value at any layer errors; but Test 17 (§11) adds 'a valid resolved layer is not shadowed by an invalid one', implying an invalid value at a lower, non-winning layer is ignored when a higher-precedence layer holds a valid value. The two leave it ambiguous whether an invalid value sitting in a non-winning layer triggers exit 2 or is silently ignored — an implementer cannot tell which resolution semantics to build.
suggestion: State explicitly that validation applies to the effective (winning) layer only: a valid higher-precedence value stands even if a lower layer holds an invalid value, while an invalid winning value errors (exit 2) with no fallback. Reword Test 17 to match that semantics.

finding: --harness-note is defined only in combination with --record ('tp review <spec> --record <file> --harness-note "<text>"'). The spec never states what happens if --harness-note is supplied without --record (e.g. on a bare 'tp review --status' or a non-recording run) — there is no round to store the note on. Exit code, hint, and whether it is a usage error or a silent no-op are all left for the implementer to guess.
suggestion: State the behavior explicitly: either reject --harness-note without --record as a usage error (exit 2) with a hint that it requires --record, or document that it is silently ignored. Add it to §6.2 and cover with a test.

finding: accepted_open is fully derivable from two values tp already emits for the same round: the round's clean flag (§3.4) and nonblocking_open (§4.2) — accepted_open is exactly (clean && nonblocking_open > 0). §4.2 emits both, and §8.4 explicitly retains BOTH under the always-on --compact path, so every compact response carries a boolean an agent can compute from the two adjacent fields. Under P3 (every output byte costs agent context) a derivable key kept in the always-on path is unearned surface.
suggestion: Drop accepted_open and let the agent derive it from clean && nonblocking_open>0, or if the boolean is kept for auditability, strip it under --compact (keep only nonblocking_open there) rather than retaining both.
